newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi to face parliament amid signs crisis averted.
newsitem.headline: Prodi to face parliament amid signs crisis averted.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi faces a vote of confidence on Thursday amid signs he will ride out a dispute with hard left allies over sending a military force to Albania that had threatened to scupper his government.

President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro told the prime minister on Wednesday evening to put his government to a confidence test after a key parliamentary ally, the Communist Refoundation party, opposed Prodi in a vote to send Italian troops.

The Chamber of Deputies (lower house) voted by an overwhelming margin to deploy the multinational force, the first of its kind to be led by Italy, but Prodi had to rely on the backing of the centre-right opposition to secure the victory.
Prodi will speak to the Senate, where Prodi's centre-left coalition has an outright majority, on Thursday at 12.30 p.m. (1030 GMT) and a confidence vote will follow in the evening.
He goes to the Chamber, where the government cannot survive without the support of Refoundation's 34 deputies, on Friday but a vote will not be held until the following day.

Prodi intended to make a full policy statement, spelling out plans to prune an inefficient welfare state and restore order to state finances in preparation for joining European economic and monetary union (EMU), political sources said.
Refoundation has signalled that despite breaking ranks over the issue of sending troops to Albania it would support the government in a confidence vote.

But coalition parties now want to seize the opportunity to determine whether Refoundation, which has repeatedly forced Prodi into embarrassing policy reversals since he has been in office, can be brought back into line.

"We must convince Communist Refoundation to support the realisation of the programme on which the government obtained its first vote of confidence and which even Refoundation voted for," Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini told reporters on Wednesday night.
Prodi staved off an immediate government crisis when the centre-right opposition said it would support a joint motion on the Albania force, whose deployment is due to start next week.
But the price for voting with the government was to force Prodi into a humiliating admission that he was not able to muster a majority of his own.
"What we are seeing is the first serious crisis of the Prodi government," Patrick McCarthy, a political scientist at Johns Hopkins University in Bologna, told Reuters Financial Television.
Opposition leader Silvio Berlusconi taunted the government in a speech to the lower house before Wednesday's vote.
"What do you intend to do? Are you going to make us put up with more months of political agony, replete with endless negotiations conducted in thrall to Communist Refoundation?" he said.
Gianfranco Fini, the leader of the far right National Alliance who is Berlusconi's main ally in opposition, said Prodi would soon cobble his majority back together.
"When you go back to parliament for the vote this (government) majority will find its unity," said Fini. "The vase that shattered into a thousand pieces will be stuck back together."

Refoundation said it would back Prodi on a confidence vote but party chairman Armando Cossutta appeared on Wednesday to spell out conditions. "If Prodi wants (to win) the confidence motion, then he should not enter into details," Cossutta said.
